title: Foreign Investors Just Poured a Record $3 Billion Into Indian Bonds in a Single Month — and the Biggest Catalyst Is Still Ahead
excerpt: India's historic decision to scrap all taxes on foreign bond investments has triggered the largest monthly inflow ever under the Fully Accessible Route, with Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index inclusion now firmly on the horizon.
body:
Foreign investors have bought a record $3 billion of Indian government bonds in June alone — nearly double the entire inflow from January through May — after New Delhi made a historic decision to scrap all taxes on foreign bond investments. And market participants say the biggest prize is still ahead: India's likely inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index, one of the most widely tracked fixed-income benchmarks in the world.

The surge, confirmed by clearing house data, marks the highest monthly net purchase since the Reserve Bank of India created its Fully Accessible Route (FAR) — the category that allows foreigners to invest in designated Indian government securities without any investment cap.

## What Changed

On June 5, Indian policymakers rolled out a sweeping package of measures designed to attract overseas capital at a time when oil prices and geopolitical tensions had strained the country's external balances.

The centrepiece: a complete exemption for foreign portfolio investors from the 12.5 percent long-term capital gains tax on government securities and the elimination of the 20 percent withholding tax on bond interest income, effective retroactively from April 1, 2026.

At the same time, the RBI broadened the pool of securities eligible under FAR to include longer-dated sovereign debt, deepening the investable universe for global funds.

"The removal of taxation on Indian government bonds will mechanically make them more interesting for global investors and will help redirecting flows towards the onshore market," said Niel Clement, a portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management.

## Why Bloomberg Matters

The real game-changer, analysts say, is what comes next. India was already included in JPMorgan's Government Bond Index-Emerging Markets (GBI-EM) in 2024, which triggered an estimated $25 billion to $30 billion in inflows over the following months. But inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Bond Index — which tracks over $68 trillion in debt and is used as a benchmark by some of the world's largest pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and insurance companies — would be a far bigger event.

Bloomberg had previously cited taxation, limited market access, and insufficient liquidity as key barriers to India's inclusion. The June measures directly address all three.

"The recent measures address some of the roadblocks to inclusion in the Bloomberg index, particularly the tax issue, as India has now aligned itself with other zero-tax sovereign issuers included in this index," said Shiv Chopra, a senior portfolio manager for emerging market fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management. "Liquidity and market depth have also now been improved."

Jennifer Taylor, head of emerging market debt at State Street Investment Management, which manages about $5.6 trillion in assets, called the changes "a game-changer for debt flows" and said Bloomberg inclusion now "appears to be on the horizon."

## The Oil Dividend

The timing has also worked in India's favour. Brent crude tumbled over 20 percent in June, retreating to levels last seen before the Iran conflict escalated, as more tankers exited the Strait of Hormuz following the initial U.S.–Iran peace deal.

Lower oil prices are a structural tailwind for India's bond market: the country imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil, and cheaper energy reduces both the fiscal deficit and inflation expectations, making government bonds more attractive on a risk-adjusted basis.

The 10-year benchmark yield fell 28 basis points over the past five weeks to 6.77 percent — its fifth consecutive weekly decline. Traders expect it to test the 6.72 percent floor this week.

## What It Means for NRI Investors

The flood of foreign capital into Indian bonds has several implications for NRI investors and the broader diaspora.

First, the tax exemptions apply equally to NRIs investing through the FPI route, making Indian government bonds one of the more attractive sovereign debt options in emerging markets on an after-tax basis.

Second, the RBI's broader package — which also includes a concessional forex swap facility for PSUs, subsidised hedging for banks raising FCNR deposits, and increased NRI equity investment limits — is designed to stabilise the rupee and improve the risk-return profile of rupee-denominated assets.

Third, if Bloomberg index inclusion materialises, it could drive an estimated $15 billion to $20 billion in additional passive inflows over the inclusion period, further compressing yields and supporting bond prices. For NRIs already holding Indian government bonds, that is a potential capital gain.

"The reforms are bearing fruit, with inflows picking up," said Lavanya Venkateswaran, executive director and senior ASEAN and India economist at OCBC Bank. "We expect more inflows on decisive policy action and easing of some external headwinds."

## The Risks

Not everything is in India's favour. Elevated hedging costs — the price of protecting against rupee depreciation — continue to eat into returns for dollar-based investors. India's monsoon season has started weakly, with June rainfall running at a 43 percent deficit, raising concerns about food inflation.

And geopolitical risks remain: while the U.S.–Iran ceasefire has calmed markets, the situation in West Asia remains fluid.

Still, the structural shift is unmistakable. India has moved from a market that global bond investors largely ignored to one that is actively courting their capital — and getting results. For NRI investors with a long-term horizon, the combination of zero-tax bonds, a falling yield curve, and the prospect of Bloomberg index inclusion represents one of the more compelling entry points in recent memory.

*Sources: Reuters, Livemint, BNP Paribas Asset Management, State Street Investment Management, OCBC Bank*
